scenes.tts: Every one of these worms kills the same one hundred and thirty-one cells. How does a body lose that many cells without leaving a mess? In healthy tissue, dead cells are cleared so fast that you rarely see a corpse.
scenes.narration: Every one of these worms kills the same 131 cells. How does a body lose that many cells without leaving a mess? In healthy tissue, dead cells are cleared so fast that you rarely see a corpse.
scenes.caption: Every one of these worms kills the same 131 cells. How does a body lose that many cells without leaving a mess? In healthy tissue, dead cells are cleared so fast that you rarely see a corpse.
scenes.visual: COLOUR MAP for the whole film (one colour per concept, same in every scene): BLUE = the plasma membrane, drawn as a thick ring, the thing to watch; TEAL = caspases, drawn as small scissor cartoons; YELLOW = phosphatidylserine, drawn as small round lipid heads on the membrane; GREEN = the phagocyte; RED = spilled contents and alarm signals; GREY = nucleus, outlines and other cells; labels in white (TEXT) or the concept colour, size 28 or larger. HOOK, no title first. Three transparent, grey worm outlines (C. elegans) wriggle slowly side by side, filling the frame width; label above in white: 'C. elegans hermaphrodites'. Inside each worm, many small grey dots (cells) drift gently. On 'the same', the same 131 dots in each worm briefly ring in BLUE, in the same positions in all three worms, then wink out one by one in the same order in every worm while a white counter in the top right ticks up to '131 of 1,090 cells'. On 'without leaving a mess?', the question appears across the top in white: 'Die without a mess?'. On 'rarely see a corpse', the camera pushes in on one worm until a single BLUE-ringed cell fills the centre; no debris is anywhere to be seen.
Title 'Sealed or Torn' fades in at the top for 2 s over the close-up cell, which keeps breathing gently (the BLUE ring pulses slowly in radius). The question text from the hook fades out beneath it.

scenes.tts: Follow one doomed cell. Its own enzymes, called caspases, switch on. They cut other proteins. The cell shrinks, its chromatin packs down, its nucleus breaks into pieces, and its surface bubbles. But watch the membrane.
scenes.narration: Follow one doomed cell. Its own enzymes, called caspases, switch on. They cut other proteins. The cell shrinks, its chromatin packs down, its nucleus breaks into pieces, and its surface bubbles. But watch the membrane.
scenes.caption: Follow one doomed cell. Its own enzymes, called caspases, switch on. They cut other proteins. The cell shrinks, its chromatin packs down, its nucleus breaks into pieces, and its surface bubbles. But watch the membrane.
scenes.visual: THE WORLD, kept for the whole film: one large round cell, centre-left, filling about 70% of frame height, outlined by a thick BLUE ring, with a GREY nucleus. Show, then name. Small TEAL scissor cartoons appear inside, first dim, then brighten and start snipping at GREY rod-shaped proteins, which fall into short pieces; label 'caspases' in TEAL appears after they are moving. On 'shrinks', the BLUE ring contracts smoothly to about two thirds of its size. On 'chromatin packs down', the grey nucleus darkens and its contents gather into dense crescents at its edge; on 'breaks into pieces', the nucleus splits into four round fragments. On 'surface bubbles', small round blebs bulge out of the BLUE ring and two pinch off as small BLUE-ringed spheres that drift a little away. On 'watch the membrane', the BLUE ring glows brighter; it is continuous everywhere, including around each bleb.

scenes.tts: It has not broken. The cell is taking itself apart, but for now every piece stays wrapped inside a closed membrane. This tidy, self-run death is called apoptosis.
scenes.narration: It has not broken. The cell is taking itself apart, but for now every piece stays wrapped inside a closed membrane. This tidy, self-run death is called apoptosis.
scenes.caption: It has not broken. The cell is taking itself apart, but for now every piece stays wrapped inside a closed membrane. This tidy, self-run death is called apoptosis.
scenes.visual: The camera circles slowly around the shrunken cell and its blebs. A small BLUE check mark travels all the way round the ring, then round each bleb, showing no gap anywhere. Inside, the TEAL scissors keep snipping (ambient motion). On 'apoptosis', the word 'apoptosis' appears in white above the cell and stays there as its label for the rest of the film.

scenes.tts: While still sealed, it can send two signals. First, a channel in its membrane opens, and small molecules puff out. They are a find-me signal. They call a phagocyte, a cell that eats other cells.
scenes.narration: While still sealed, it can send two signals. First, a channel in its membrane opens, and small molecules puff out. They are a find-me signal. They call a phagocyte, a cell that eats other cells.
scenes.caption: While still sealed, it can send two signals. First, a channel in its membrane opens, and small molecules puff out. They are a find-me signal. They call a phagocyte, a cell that eats other cells.
scenes.visual: A small gap-free channel (a short BLUE tube through the ring) appears on the right side of the cell; the ring around it stays closed. From it, small white dots puff out in a steady stream and spread rightwards as a fading cloud; label 'find-me' in white beside the cloud. On 'call a phagocyte', a large GREEN cell with a wavy edge enters from the far right edge of the frame, crawling slowly up the cloud toward the dying cell. Label 'phagocyte' in GREEN on it.

scenes.tts: Second, a lipid called phosphatidylserine normally sits mostly on the membrane's inner face. The caspases cut the membrane proteins that control which face it sits on. Now it appears on the outer face. That is the eat-me flag.
scenes.narration: Second, a lipid called phosphatidylserine normally sits mostly on the membrane's inner face. The caspases cut the membrane proteins that control which face it sits on. Now it appears on the outer face. That is the eat-me flag.
scenes.caption: Second, a lipid called phosphatidylserine normally sits mostly on the membrane's inner face. The caspases cut the membrane proteins that control which face it sits on. Now it appears on the outer face. That is the eat-me flag.
scenes.visual: Zoom into a short arc of the BLUE ring, drawn now as a band with an inner face and an outer face (two thin BLUE lines; inside and outside labelled). Small YELLOW round heads line the inner face, with one or two already on the outer face (mostly inside, not only). Embedded in the band sit TWO small generic GREY membrane proteins (unlabelled blocks; no names, no pump or door shapes: the text's Predict asks about them). On 'cut the membrane proteins', a TEAL scissor snips each: one switches into a lipid-mixing state (a gap that lets heads pass both ways) and the other, which had been moving heads inward, switches off. On 'Now it appears on the outer face', only after both changes, the YELLOW heads move across to the outer face one by one. Zoom back out: the whole cell is now dotted with YELLOW heads on its outer surface; label 'eat-me' in YELLOW. The GREEN phagocyte keeps crawling closer the whole time.

scenes.tts: Here is the idea to carry. In apoptosis, the membrane holds while the cell takes itself apart. That buys time for a phagocyte to eat it before anything leaks.
scenes.narration: Here is the idea to carry. In apoptosis, the membrane holds while the cell takes itself apart. That buys time for a phagocyte to eat it before anything leaks.
scenes.caption: Here is the idea to carry. In apoptosis, the membrane holds while the cell takes itself apart. That buys time for a phagocyte to eat it before anything leaks.
scenes.visual: The scene holds the full world: shrunken cell with BLUE ring, YELLOW heads outside, white find-me cloud, GREEN phagocyte now nearly touching. Across the top, in white, the idea writes itself on: 'Holds while taken apart'. On 'takes itself apart', the TEAL scissors flash; on 'membrane holds', the BLUE ring glows; on 'buys time', a small white timer arc sweeps once around the ring (schematic, no numbers); on 'before anything leaks', the GREEN phagocyte edges closer and no RED appears.

scenes.tts: The phagocyte arrives and recognises the flag. In the simplest picture, it wraps around the whole cell and swallows it. A lysosome digests it. Nothing spills. That is why you rarely see a corpse.
scenes.narration: The phagocyte arrives and recognises the flag. In the simplest picture, it wraps around the whole cell and swallows it. A lysosome digests it. Nothing spills. That is why you rarely see a corpse.
scenes.caption: The phagocyte arrives and recognises the flag. In the simplest picture, it wraps around the whole cell and swallows it. A lysosome digests it. Nothing spills. That is why you rarely see a corpse.
scenes.visual: The GREEN phagocyte touches the YELLOW heads; its edge sends out two arms that flow around the BLUE-ringed cell and its blebs and close behind them, so the whole dying cell, ring intact, now sits inside the GREEN cell. A small GREY sphere labelled 'lysosome' merges with it, and the swallowed cell shrinks and fades to nothing. No RED appears anywhere at any point. On 'rarely see a corpse', cut back (a smooth zoom out) to the worm from the hook: one more BLUE dot winks out with no debris left behind.

scenes.tts: Now put the same kind of dying cell in a dish, where no phagocyte will come. Time passes. What happens to its membrane?
scenes.narration: Now put the same kind of dying cell in a dish, where no phagocyte will come. Time passes. What happens to its membrane?
scenes.caption: Now put the same kind of dying cell in a dish, where no phagocyte will come. Time passes. What happens to its membrane?
scenes.visual: A dish appears: a flat GREY circle seen from above, fills the frame. In it sits a new shrunken apoptotic cell, BLUE ring intact, YELLOW heads outside, TEAL scissors inside. No GREEN cell anywhere. A small white clock in the corner labelled 'time (schematic)' starts sweeping. On 'What happens to its membrane?', a white question card appears at the top: 'What happens to the ring?' and the BLUE ring pulses slowly.

Thinking pause. The question card 'What happens to the ring?' stays on screen. The clock keeps sweeping slowly; the BLUE ring keeps a slow pulse; the YELLOW heads shimmer gently. Nothing else changes.

scenes.tts: Often, it fails. The membrane that held through the early stages now leaks, and the contents spill. This late leak is called secondary necrosis. In a tissue, a phagocyte usually gets there first.
scenes.narration: Often, it fails. The membrane that held through the early stages now leaks, and the contents spill. This late leak is called secondary necrosis. In a tissue, a phagocyte usually gets there first.
scenes.caption: Often, it fails. The membrane that held through the early stages now leaks, and the contents spill. This late leak is called secondary necrosis. In a tissue, a phagocyte usually gets there first.
scenes.visual: The question card fades. On 'Often, it fails', the BLUE ring thins at two points and opens; RED contents seep out through the gaps and spread across the dish floor. Label 'secondary necrosis' in RED appears under the cell. On 'In a tissue', a small inset in the upper right replays the eaten-sealed ending from the earlier scene in miniature (GREEN swallows BLUE ring, no RED), with the label 'tissue' under it and 'dish' under the main picture.

scenes.tts: Some cells die the other way round. This one swells, and its membrane tears early. Its contents spill at once, including alarm signals. These can call in the immune system and cause inflammation. This messy death is called necrosis.
scenes.narration: Some cells die the other way round. This one swells, and its membrane tears early. Its contents spill at once, including alarm signals. These can call in the immune system and cause inflammation. This messy death is called necrosis.
scenes.caption: Some cells die the other way round. This one swells, and its membrane tears early. Its contents spill at once, including alarm signals. These can call in the immune system and cause inflammation. This messy death is called necrosis.
scenes.visual: Clear the dish. A second cell appears on the right half of the frame, same size and style as the first, BLUE ring, GREY nucleus, but no TEAL scissors inside. Show first: it swells smoothly to about 1.4 times its size, its small GREY organelles swelling too, while the nucleus stays whole. On 'tears early', the BLUE ring rips open along one side with jagged edges. RED contents gush out at once; among them a few larger RED dots labelled 'alarm signals'. On 'immune system', two small GREY immune cells hurry in from the edge toward the RED; a soft RED glow labelled 'inflammation' spreads around them. On 'necrosis', the word 'necrosis' appears above this cell in white.

scenes.tts: Tearing does not mean accident: some tearing deaths are genetic programs too. In its simplest form, the difference is timing. Apoptosis keeps the membrane intact early. Necrotic deaths generally open it early.
scenes.narration: Tearing does not mean accident: some tearing deaths are genetic programs too. In its simplest form, the difference is timing. Apoptosis keeps the membrane intact early. Necrotic deaths generally open it early.
scenes.caption: Tearing does not mean accident: some tearing deaths are genetic programs too. In its simplest form, the difference is timing. Apoptosis keeps the membrane intact early. Necrotic deaths generally open it early.
scenes.visual: Bring back the apoptotic cell on the left half, labelled 'apoptosis', with its BLUE ring intact and the GREEN phagocyte beside it; the torn necrotic cell stays on the right with its RED spill and label 'necrosis'. On 'programs too', three small white gene-tag cartoons (labelled boxes, no names) appear briefly beside the torn cell and fade. On 'the difference is timing', a white timeline (schematic, no numbers) slides in under both cells, labelled 'early' at its left end. On 'intact early', a BLUE tick under the left cell at 'early' shows the ring whole. On 'open it early', a RED tick under the right cell at 'early' shows the ring open. Do not show the left cell being swallowed here.

scenes.tts: So back to the worm. Its doomed cells are usually eaten by neighbouring cells before they spill. A membrane that holds until the meal often makes for a quieter death.
scenes.narration: So back to the worm. Its doomed cells are usually eaten by neighbouring cells before they spill. A membrane that holds until the meal often makes for a quieter death.
scenes.caption: So back to the worm. Its doomed cells are usually eaten by neighbouring cells before they spill. A membrane that holds until the meal often makes for a quieter death.
scenes.visual: Smooth zoom out from the two-cell comparison back to the three worms from the hook. In one worm, a BLUE-ringed cell shrinks and is engulfed by a neighbouring GREY cell that flushes GREEN at its edge; no RED anywhere. The white counter from the hook shows '131 of 1,090 cells' again. On 'a quieter death', the left and right cells from the previous scene reappear small at the bottom, side by side, labelled 'sealed and eaten' and 'torn and spilled'.

End card on the dark background, white text centred: 'Apoptosis keeps the membrane intact early, often until the cell is eaten.' A thin BLUE ring is drawn slowly around the sentence and stays closed. Small line beneath in GREY: 'biochemistrypedia.com'.
